disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Vendor-neutral; no affiliation with any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original.

choices: DATE_TRUNC the timestamp to month, GROUP BY the truncated month — time-series analysis needs a consistent time grain before aggregating
GROUP BY the raw timestamp — each second is a group
Time grain doesn't matter for trends
Use string formatting for months
scenarios.hint: What does one row of the result represent — a second, or a month?
scenarios.prompt: How do you build a monthly trend?
scenarios.situation: 'Signups per month' — a junior analyst groups by the raw timestamp and gets millions of groups.
scenarios.title: The timestamp groups
scenarios.why: Time-series analysis starts by choosing the grain: DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) buckets timestamps to month starts, then GROUP BY aggregates. Without truncation, every distinct timestamp is its own group — noise, not trend. (Syntax varies: DATE_TRUNC in Postgres, DATETRUNC in T-SQL, DATE_FORMAT in MySQL — the concept is universal.) Also mind time zones: truncate in the business's time zone, not UTC, or month boundaries shift.

choices: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) — unique users; COUNT(*) counts events; the ratio is events per user — know which the question asks
COUNT(*) — it counts users
They are the same when grouped
COUNT(user_id) counts unique users
evidence:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', ts) AS day,
 COUNT(*) AS events,
 COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users
FROM clicks GROUP BY 1;
scenarios.hint: If one user clicks 50 times, how many 'users' is that — and how many 'events'?
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference, and why does it matter?
scenarios.situation: 'Daily active users' computed with COUNT(*) shows 10x the known user base — power users dominate.
scenarios.title: The active-user inflation
scenarios.why: COUNT(*) counts rows (events); COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts unique users. 'Active users' = distinct users; 'engagement' might = events. Mixing them up inflates DAU by the activity of power users. The events-per-user ratio (COUNT(*)/COUNT(DISTINCT)) is itself a useful metric — but only when you know which numerator and denominator you're using.

choices: Cohort retention: GROUP BY signup month (cohort), then compute % active in each subsequent month — retention curves reveal whether the product keeps users
Overall monthly actives — it shows retention
Cohort analysis needs no SQL
Retention equals 1 minus churn always
evidence:
WITH cohorts AS (
 SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_at) AS cohort FROM users)
SELECT c.cohort,
 DATE_TRUNC('month', a.active_at) AS m,
 COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active
FROM cohorts c JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = c.user_id
GROUP BY 1, 2;
scenarios.hint: 'Users who signed up in January, what % were active in March?' — what two groupings do you need?
scenarios.prompt: How do you measure whether the product retains users?
scenarios.situation: Total signups grow, but nobody knows if users stick around. Overall actives look flat.
scenarios.title: The leaky bucket
scenarios.why: Cohort retention: group users by signup period (the cohort), then track each cohort's activity over subsequent periods — producing retention curves. Flat overall actives + growing signups = churn masking growth (the leaky bucket). Cohort curves show whether newer cohorts retain better (product improving) or all cohorts decay the same (structural problem). It's the core product-health analysis.

choices: Funnel with step-by-step conversion: count users reaching each stage (ordered), compute conversion between consecutive steps — drop-off pinpoints friction
Total conversions only — funnels add nothing
Funnel steps can be in any order
Conversion rates need no denominators
evidence:
WITH steps AS (
 SELECT user_id,
  MAX(CASE WHEN event='view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS viewed,
  MAX(CASE WHEN event='cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted,
  MAX(CASE WHEN event='buy' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS bought
 FROM events GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS users,
 SUM(viewed) AS viewed, SUM(carted) AS carted, SUM(bought) AS bought
FROM steps;
scenarios.hint: To find where users drop off, what do you need at each stage — and in what order?
scenarios.prompt: How do you build a conversion funnel in SQL?
scenarios.situation: 'Where do shoppers drop off?' — the team has event data but no funnel.
scenarios.title: The leaky funnel
scenarios.why: Funnel = ordered stages with per-stage user counts; conversion = stage_n / stage_{n-1}. The conditional-aggregation pattern (MAX(CASE WHEN event=...) per user) builds the funnel in one pass. The biggest drop-off between consecutive steps is where friction lives. Caveats: enforce event ordering (cart before buy), define the time window (session? 7 days?), and segment (mobile vs desktop funnels differ wildly).

choices: Window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1 — latest row per user without collapsing; or DISTINCT ON / QUALIFY per dialect
GROUP BY user_id with MAX(ts) — then join back for the full row
ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 1 — gives one user's latest
Latest row per user is impossible in SQL
scenarios.hint: Which pattern keeps the full row of each user's latest event?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get each user's current subscription status?
scenarios.situation: A subscriptions table has history rows per user. 'Current status per user' needs the latest row each.
scenarios.title: The current status
scenarios.why: ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by user ordered by time desc, filter rn=1 — the standard 'latest per group' pattern, returning full rows. (GROUP BY + MAX gets the timestamp but needs a self-join for the rest of the row.) Dialect shortcuts exist (Postgres DISTINCT ON, Snowflake/BigQuery QUALIFY). Every analyst needs this pattern — slowly-changing entity state is everywhere.

choices: Percent of total: SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () — window over the grouped result; or ratio-to-report patterns per dialect
Subquery computing the grand total, joined back — the only way
Percentages can't be computed in SQL
Divide by COUNT(*) instead
scenarios.hint: After GROUP BY, what does SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () compute?
scenarios.prompt: How do you compute each region's share of total?
scenarios.situation: 'Each region's % of total sales' — the analyst writes two queries and divides in a spreadsheet.
scenarios.title: The share of total
scenarios.why: Window functions evaluate after GROUP BY: SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () = grand total over the grouped rows, so each row's share = its sum / grand total. One query, no spreadsheet round-trip. (Some dialects need a subquery/CTE: compute grouped sums, then window over them.) It's the 'percent of total' and 'running share' foundation.

choices: Pivot table — drag-and-drop grouping/summarizing for exploration; formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS) for fixed, auditable calculations
Formulas for everything — pivots aren't reproducible
Pivot tables can't handle large data
VLOOKUP for aggregation
scenarios.hint: Exploring 'sales by region by quarter' interactively — formulas or drag-and-drop?
scenarios.prompt: When do you reach for a pivot table vs formulas?
scenarios.situation: An analyst writes 40 SUMIFS formulas to slice sales by region × quarter. The VP asks for 'by product too' — 40 more formulas.
scenarios.title: The formula sprawl
scenarios.why: Pivot tables are the exploration tool: drag fields to rows/columns/values, slice interactively, no formula maintenance. Formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS/XLOOKUP) suit fixed, repeatable calculations that must be auditable cell-by-cell. Rule: exploring → pivot; productionizing a fixed report → formulas (or better, SQL). 40 SUMIFS is a pivot table crying for help.

choices: XLOOKUP (or INDEX+MATCH) — looks left or right, exact match by default, handles missing gracefully; VLOOKUP only looks right and breaks when columns move
VLOOKUP — the standard; limitations are fine
VLOOKUP can look left with a flag
Lookup direction doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: The lookup column is to the RIGHT of the return column — which function handles that?
scenarios.prompt: Why has XLOOKUP replaced VLOOKUP?
scenarios.situation: A VLOOKUP breaks every time someone inserts a column; another needs to look left of the key column.
scenarios.title: The broken VLOOKUP
scenarios.why: VLOOKUP: searches the first column, returns from a column index to the right — brittle (column inserts shift the index) and one-directional. XLOOKUP (or INDEX+MATCH): separate lookup and return arrays — looks any direction, exact match default, built-in if-not-found handling. For analysts still on VLOOKUP: the upgrade removes an entire bug class.

choices: Clean first: TRIM whitespace, standardize case, fix date formats, split/merge columns, remove duplicates — analysis on dirty data is fiction
Analyze first; cleaning is optional
Dirty data averages out
Whitespace doesn't affect matching
scenarios.hint: 'New York' vs 'new york ' vs 'NEW YORK' — how many distinct values does the pivot see?
scenarios.prompt: What is the cleaning checklist before analysis?
scenarios.situation: A pivot shows 3 versions of 'New York'; dates mix US/EU formats; duplicates inflate counts.
scenarios.title: The dirty column
scenarios.why: Cleaning checklist: TRIM whitespace, UPPER/LOWER standardization, consistent date parsing (TEXTSPLIT or DATEVALUE with known format), dedupe (Remove Duplicates on key columns), handle blanks vs zeros explicitly. 'New York' × 3 = 3 groups in the pivot. Garbage in, gospel out is the analyst's original sin — clean before you conclude.

choices: One row per observation, one column per variable (tidy data); headers in row 1, no merged cells, no totals rows mixed into data — structure for analysis, format for presentation separately
Merged headers look professional — keep them
Totals rows inside the data are fine
Multiple tables per sheet is tidiest
scenarios.hint: Can a pivot table read a sheet with merged headers and subtotal rows mixed in?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a spreadsheet analysis-ready?
scenarios.situation: A 'report' sheet with merged headers, subtotal rows, and notes in cells can't be pivoted or imported.
scenarios.title: The unpivotable sheet
scenarios.why: Tidy structure: row 1 = single-row headers, one observation per row, one variable per column, no merged cells, no embedded totals/notes. Presentation formatting (merges, subtotals) belongs on a separate presentation sheet fed by formulas — never mixed into the data. If a pivot can't read it, it's not data, it's a picture of data.

choices: Spreadsheets are for exploration and small, manual work — beyond ~1M rows, multi-source joins, or scheduled refreshes, move to SQL/BI; version control is the hard limit
Spreadsheets scale infinitely
Version control works fine with emailed files
1M rows is plenty for any analysis
scenarios.hint: The file is emailed as 'final_v7_REALLY_FINAL.xlsx' — what broke?
scenarios.prompt: When do you outgrow spreadsheets?
scenarios.situation: A 2M-row 'analysis' spreadsheet crashes; three versions circulate by email; nobody can reproduce last month's numbers.
scenarios.title: The final_v7 spreadsheet
scenarios.why: Spreadsheet limits: row caps (~1M), no real version control (email chains), manual steps that don't reproduce, silent formula errors at scale. Graduate to SQL (data size, joins), BI tools (scheduled refresh, governed metrics), and version-controlled code when: data exceeds comfortable size, the analysis repeats on a schedule, or more than one person must reproduce it. Spreadsheets are the sketchpad, not the system.

choices: Data validation rules + conditional formatting for outliers + protected ranges — prevent bad input, highlight anomalies, lock formulas
More training for data enterers
Validation is unnecessary for internal sheets
Conditional formatting is decoration
scenarios.hint: A typo'd date breaks the monthly rollup — where should that typo have been caught?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make a shared input sheet trustworthy?
scenarios.situation: A team expense tracker: typos in dates and categories break the summary; someone overwrote a formula.
scenarios.title: The shared tracker
scenarios.why: Prevent, don't fix: data validation dropdowns constrain categories, date validation constrains formats, conditional formatting flags outliers/duplicates visually, and sheet protection locks formula cells while leaving inputs editable. A shared sheet without validation is a data-quality incident waiting for a deadline.

choices: Start the y-axis at zero for bar charts (bar length encodes value); line charts for trends can zoom — truncated bar axes exaggerate tiny differences into dramatic gaps
Truncated axes are always fine
Bar charts should never start at zero
Axis choice doesn't affect perception
scenarios.hint: Two bars: 98 vs 100. With the axis starting at 95, how big does the difference look?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the y-axis baseline matter?
scenarios.situation: A bar chart with the y-axis starting at 90 makes a 2% difference look like a 10x gap. Marketing loves it.
scenarios.title: The dramatic bar chart
scenarios.why: Bar length encodes value — truncating the axis breaks the encoding, turning small differences into visual lies. Bars: start at zero. Lines (position encodes value, not length) may zoom to show variation — but label clearly. The analyst's job: choose the axis that informs, not the one that impresses. When someone asks for the truncated version, show both and explain.

choices: Line chart for trends over time, bar for comparisons, scatter for relationships, histogram for distributions — and almost never pie (humans judge angles poorly)
Pie charts for everything — they're friendly
3D charts add clarity
One chart type fits all data
scenarios.hint: 'Sales over 12 months' vs 'market share' vs 'price vs demand' — which shape answers each?
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose the chart type?
scenarios.situation: A deck uses pie charts for trends, 3D bars for comparisons, and a table for a distribution.
scenarios.title: The chart-type roulette
scenarios.why: Match encoding to question: trends over time → line; categorical comparison → bar; two-variable relationship → scatter; distribution shape → histogram; part-of-whole (few parts) → stacked bar beats pie (angle judgment is weak; length judgment is strong). 3D distorts every encoding it touches. The chart is an argument — pick the one that makes the true pattern easiest to see.

choices: Direct labels / annotations on the chart — put the numbers where the eye already is; legends force eye-tennis between chart and key
Legends are mandatory for all charts
Colors alone communicate values
Annotations clutter charts
scenarios.hint: With 8 similar colors and a legend, how long does it take to find 'Northeast'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make a multi-series chart readable?
scenarios.situation: An 8-region line chart with a legend: readers can't tell which line is which.
scenarios.title: The legend hunt
scenarios.why: Direct labeling (series names at line ends, values on bars) removes the legend-lookup round trip — the eye stays on the data. Legends fail past ~4 similar series. Annotate the insight too ('Launch spike', 'Policy change') — a chart without the 'so what' labeled is a puzzle, not a message. Reduce the reader's work to zero.

choices: Colorblind-safe palettes, sufficient contrast, never color-as-only-encoding (add labels/patterns) — ~8% of men have color-vision deficiency
Rainbow palettes maximize information
Red-green is fine; everyone sees it
Accessibility doesn't apply to internal dashboards
scenarios.hint: If red and green look identical to the reader, what does your 'good vs bad' encoding say?
scenarios.prompt: What are the color rules for dashboards?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard encodes good/bad as red/green only. A colorblind stakeholder misreads it.
scenarios.title: The red-green dashboard
scenarios.why: ~1 in 12 men has color-vision deficiency — red/green as the sole encoding excludes them. Rules: colorblind-safe palettes (blue/orange, not red/green), color never the only channel (add labels, shapes, or position), sufficient contrast for text. Accessibility isn't polish; it's correctness for part of your audience.

choices: Small multiples — same chart repeated per segment at the same scale; comparison happens visually, instantly
One chart with 20 series
Separate dashboards per segment
Animation between segments
scenarios.hint: 12 regions × monthly trend — one spaghetti chart, or 12 small identical charts?
scenarios.prompt: How do you compare many segments?
scenarios.situation: A 20-series line chart is spaghetti. Splitting into 20 slides loses comparison.
scenarios.title: The spaghetti chart
scenarios.why: Small multiples: the same chart repeated per segment, identical scales, in a grid — the eye compares shapes instantly. One overloaded chart is unreadable; separate pages break comparison. Same scale is the discipline (different scales lie). For segment comparison, small multiples are the most information-dense honest layout.

choices: Declutter: remove gridlines/borders/3D, highlight the data (one accent color for the insight, gray for context), maximize data-ink ratio
More elements look more professional
Every chart needs a border and background shading
Data-ink ratio is aesthetic trivia
scenarios.hint: What remains when you delete everything that isn't data?
scenarios.prompt: What is the decluttering discipline?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard is heavy borders, gridlines, gradients, and 3D — the data is hard to find.
scenarios.title: The chartjunk
scenarios.why: Data-ink ratio: maximize ink spent on data, minimize on decoration. Remove: heavy gridlines, borders, backgrounds, 3D effects, redundant labels. Then highlight: one accent color draws the eye to the insight; everything else recedes to gray. A clean chart isn't minimalism for style — it's respect for the reader's attention.

choices: Median (robust to skew) alongside the mean — report both, and show the distribution; the mean alone lies about skewed data
Mean is always the right 'average'
Drop the outliers to fix the mean
Median hides information
scenarios.hint: Which single number describes 'the typical employee's salary' here?
scenarios.prompt: Which average, and why does the choice matter?
scenarios.situation: 'Average salary is $400k!' — the mean includes the CEO's $2.5M. Employees are confused.
scenarios.title: The $400k average
scenarios.why: The mean is pulled by skew; the median (50th percentile) resists it. For skewed distributions (income, home prices, deal sizes), the median describes the typical case; the mean describes the total-per-head. Report both + the distribution shape. Choosing the mean for skewed data isn't wrong math — it's wrong communication.

choices: Correlation ≠ causation — ice-cream sales correlate with drownings (both rise in summer); look for confounders, and test with experiments
Correlation proves causation with enough data
Confounders don't matter with big data
A/B tests are unnecessary when correlation is strong
scenarios.hint: What third variable rises in summer alongside both ice cream and drownings?
scenarios.prompt: What is the analytical failure?
scenarios.situation: 'Users who use feature X retain better!' — the team ships more X. Retention doesn't move. Power users adopt every feature.
scenarios.title: The feature fallacy
scenarios.why: Correlation: X-users retain more. Causation would need: X causes retention. The confounder: power users both adopt features and retain — X is a marker of engagement, not its cause. Before acting on correlation: name plausible confounders, segment (does X help within engagement bands?), and run an experiment. Observational wins are hypotheses, not conclusions.

choices: Randomized A/B test with a pre-registered metric, sufficient sample size/power, and a fixed runtime — then check statistical significance, not just the raw lift
Ship it; the 5% lift is obvious
Run the test until it looks significant, then stop
Sample size doesn't matter with a big lift
scenarios.hint: If you peek daily and stop when it's significant, what happens to your false-positive rate?
scenarios.prompt: How do you run the test properly?
scenarios.situation: A button change shows +5% conversion after 3 days. The team wants to ship; nobody computed power or significance.
scenarios.title: The 5% lift
scenarios.why: Proper A/B: randomize, pre-register the primary metric and runtime, size for statistical power (enough users to detect a meaningful effect), then read significance at the end. Sins: peeking/stopping early (inflates false positives), tiny samples (noise), and multiple metrics without correction (one will 'win' by chance). +5% on 200 users is noise; on 200k it's signal. Do the math before shipping.

choices: Selection bias — survey respondents self-select (happy/angry extremes); the sample doesn't represent all users. Weight, or better, sample randomly
Survey results are representative by default
More responses fix bias
Bias only matters in small samples
scenarios.hint: Who bothers to answer a satisfaction survey — the delighted, the furious, or the indifferent middle?
scenarios.prompt: Why might the 4.8/5 satisfaction score be misleading?
scenarios.situation: A satisfaction survey (2% response rate) scores 4.8/5, but churn is rising and support tickets grow.
scenarios.title: The 4.8 paradox
scenarios.why: 2% response = self-selected extremes; the indifferent middle (often the churners) doesn't answer. The score measures 'respondents', not 'users'. Fixes: random sampling with follow-up, compare respondent vs population characteristics, weight responses, and triangulate with behavioral data (tickets, churn). A biased sample doesn't improve with size — 100k biased responses are still biased.

choices: Base rates — 1% defect rate means most positives are false positives even with a '99% accurate' test; always combine test accuracy with the base rate (Bayes)
99% accurate means 99% of positives are true
Base rates don't matter with good tests
False positives are rare by definition
evidence:
1000 shipments, 1% truly late (10). Test: 99% accurate.
→ ~10 true positives + ~10 false positives → P(late | flagged) ≈ 50%
scenarios.hint: Out of 1000 shipments with 10 truly late, how many false alarms does a 99%-accurate flag raise?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the '99% accurate' alert wrong half the time?
scenarios.situation: A '99% accurate' late-shipment predictor flags orders; half the flags are wrong. The team blames the model.
scenarios.title: The base-rate trap
scenarios.why: With a 1% base rate, even 99% accuracy yields ~equal true and false positives (10 real lates caught, ~10 false alarms from 990 on-time). P(late|flagged) ≈ 50%. The model is fine; the expectation ignored Bayes. Lesson: rare-event prediction needs either much higher precision or a workflow that tolerates false alarms. Always condition on the base rate.

choices: Simpson's paradox — the aggregate reverses the segment trends; segment before concluding (e.g., by traffic source/device)
Aggregates are always trustworthy
The segments must be wrong
Paradoxes don't occur in real data
evidence:
Overall: new design converts better (5% vs 4%).
By segment: old design wins on mobile AND on desktop.
scenarios.hint: What if the new design got 90% desktop traffic (high-converting) and the old got 90% mobile?
scenarios.prompt: How can the new design win overall but lose in every segment?
scenarios.situation: Overall conversion favors the new design, but it loses within mobile and within desktop separately.
scenarios.title: The paradox
scenarios.why: Simpson's paradox: a lurking variable (traffic mix) reverses the aggregate. If the new design received mostly high-converting desktop traffic, its overall rate is inflated by mix, not merit. Within each segment, the old design wins. Rule: always segment by known confounders (device, source, region) before trusting an aggregate — the overall number can lie while every segment tells the truth.

choices: Semantic layer — define each metric once (SQL/model), certify it, and have every dashboard consume the definition; 'revenue' has one author and one meaning
Each dashboard defines its own metrics — flexibility
Semantic layers slow down analysis
One definition per dashboard is fine
scenarios.hint: Who decides what 'active user' means — each dashboard author, or one governed definition?
scenarios.prompt: How do you end 'three dashboards, three revenues'?
scenarios.situation: Three dashboards show three different revenue numbers. Each defines revenue slightly differently.
scenarios.title: The three revenues
scenarios.why: A semantic layer centralizes metric definitions: one governed 'revenue' (with its exact logic, filters, and grain), consumed by all dashboards and self-service. Dashboards become presentations of certified metrics, not independent computations. Without it, every dashboard is a new opinion. With it, arguments move from 'whose number is right' to 'is the definition right' — a much better argument.

choices: Aggregate/navigation design: pre-aggregate at common grains, limit default date ranges, push filters to the source, and monitor query performance — dashboards must feel instant
Load raw billions of rows into the dashboard
Performance is the warehouse's problem
Users tolerate 2-minute dashboard loads
scenarios.hint: A dashboard scanning 5B rows per load — what computes once instead of per-view?
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep dashboards fast over big data?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard over billions of rows takes 90 seconds to load. Users stop using it.
scenarios.title: The 90-second dashboard
scenarios.why: Dashboard performance discipline: pre-aggregate to the dashboard's grain (materialized/aggregate tables), default to sane date ranges (not 'all time'), ensure filters hit partitioned/indexed columns, and cache. A dashboard is a serving layer — it should query aggregates, not raw fact tables. If the dashboard queries billions of rows per interaction, the modeling failed, not the tool.

choices: Certified vs sandbox: governed, certified datasets for official metrics; sandbox/exploratory space for ad-hoc work — with clear labeling so nobody mistakes one for the other
All self-service, no governance — fastest
Lock everything down — no self-service
Governance and self-service are opposites
scenarios.hint: How do you let analysts explore freely without letting experiments become 'official numbers'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you balance self-service with trust?
scenarios.situation: Analysts build on raw tables; executives quote exploratory numbers as fact. Locking everything down kills productivity.
scenarios.title: The wild-west BI
scenarios.why: Two-tier: certified datasets (governed, documented, tested — the official numbers) and a sandbox (raw/exploratory — clearly labeled 'unverified'). Analysts explore freely in the sandbox; promotion to certified requires review. Labeling is the keystone: every dashboard states its certification status. Self-service without governance produces confident wrong numbers; governance without self-service produces shadow BI.

choices: Row-level security — filter data by the viewer's identity/role in the BI tool or semantic layer; one dashboard, many views, enforced centrally
One dashboard per team — simplest secure
RLS is just hiding tabs
Security can be handled by telling users not to look
scenarios.hint: The CEO and a regional manager open the same dashboard — who should see whose numbers?
scenarios.prompt: How does one dashboard serve many audiences securely?
scenarios.situation: A sales dashboard must show each rep only their territory, managers their region, execs everything.
scenarios.title: The one-dashboard rule
scenarios.why: Row-level security applies data filters by viewer identity (role, territory mapping) — one dashboard definition, personalized data, enforced in the platform (not in the user's hands). Cloning dashboards per audience multiplies maintenance and leaks via stale copies. RLS belongs in the semantic layer/platform so it's consistent across every surface.

choices: Scheduled refresh aligned to data SLAs + data-driven alerts (alert when a metric crosses a threshold, not just 'dashboard updated') — push the insight, don't just publish it
Refresh everything hourly — fresher is always better
Alerts on every data change
Manual refresh is fine
scenarios.hint: Nobody opens the dashboard — how does the insight reach them?
scenarios.prompt: How do dashboards stay fresh and actually seen?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard refreshes nightly, but the metric it tracks moves intraday. Nobody checks it anyway.
scenarios.title: The unseen dashboard
scenarios.why: Match refresh to the data's SLA and decision cadence (intraday metric → intraday refresh; daily KPI → daily). Then invert the model: data-driven alerts push exceptions to stakeholders (Slack/email when churn spikes) instead of hoping they open the dashboard. Dashboards are for investigation; alerts are for attention. An unopened dashboard is a write-only report.

choices: Version the dashboard definitions, document metric logic, and review changes — dashboards are code; treat them like it
Dashboards don't need version control
Screenshots document dashboards
Only the data needs governance
scenarios.hint: Who changed the revenue filter last Tuesday, and can you get the old version back?
scenarios.prompt: How do you operate dashboards like software?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard's numbers change; nobody knows who edited it or what changed.
scenarios.title: The mystery edit
scenarios.why: Dashboards are production artifacts: version their definitions (BI tools with git integration, or exported definitions in version control), document metric logic alongside, require review for certified dashboards, and keep a changelog. 'Someone edited the filter' shouldn't be a mystery — it should be a commit. Operate dashboards with the same discipline as the pipelines feeding them.

choices: Pyramid principle — lead with the conclusion/recommendation, then supporting evidence, then details; executives decide, they don't explore
Build suspense: background, methodology, then the answer on slide 20
Chronological order is clearest
Details first, conclusion last

scenarios.situation: A 30-slide deck buries the recommendation on slide 28. The exec stops paying attention at slide 5.
scenarios.title: The buried lede
scenarios.why: Pyramid principle: answer first ('We should do X'), then the 2-3 supporting reasons, then details as backup. Executives need the decision up front; they drill into evidence only where they doubt. Chronological 'here's what I did' structures serve the analyst's journey, not the reader's decision. Lead with the 'so what', earn the right to the 'how'.

choices: One message per chart, stated in the title — 'Churn spikes after the price increase' not 'Churn by month'; the title is the takeaway
Cute titles: 'Churn analysis'
Titles should describe the chart type
Takeaways belong in the appendix

scenarios.prompt: What makes a chart title effective?
scenarios.situation: A deck of charts titled 'Revenue by segment', 'Churn by month' — readers must deduce each point themselves.
scenarios.title: The descriptive titles
scenarios.why: Action titles state the insight ('Enterprise churn doubled after onboarding changes'), not the content ('Churn by segment'). Each chart makes one point; the title is that point. Descriptive titles outsource interpretation to the busiest readers — they'll get it wrong or skip it. Write the title last, after you know the message.

choices: Show the uncertainty: ranges, confidence intervals, sensitivity ('if X, then Y') — and state what would change the conclusion; false precision destroys trust when you're wrong
Point estimates only — ranges look indecisive
Hide the caveats; they'll ask if needed
Uncertainty means the analysis failed
scenarios.hint: 'Revenue will grow 12%' vs 'likely 8–15%, driven by enterprise renewals' — which survives being slightly wrong?
scenarios.prompt: How do you present uncertain findings honestly?
scenarios.situation: A forecast is presented as a single number. It's wrong; stakeholders stop trusting the team's numbers.
scenarios.title: The false precision
scenarios.why: Honest uncertainty: ranges instead of point estimates, key assumptions stated, sensitivity to drivers ('±3 points if renewal rate moves 5%'), and pre-mortem ('what would change this conclusion'). False precision borrows trust and repays it with interest when wrong. Decision-makers can act on ranges; they can't act on a number nobody believes.

choices: Context → complication → resolution: set the business context, name the tension, then the recommendation — a narrative arc, not a data dump
Data dump in appendix order
Start with methodology — credibility first
Narratives are for marketing, not analysis

scenarios.prompt: How do you turn analysis into a story?
scenarios.situation: A readout lists 15 findings. Stakeholders remember none and ask 'so what do we do?'
scenarios.title: The 15 findings
scenarios.why: Narrative arc: context (what's happening), complication (the tension/change), resolution (what we should do). Fifteen findings with no arc = fifteen forgettable facts. Group findings into 2-3 insights that build to one recommendation. Stories are memory structures — the same data, shaped as tension→resolution, gets remembered and acted on.

choices: Recommendation tied to evidence with trade-offs named: 'Do X because [evidence]; costs [Y]; if [assumption] is wrong, do Z' — a decision, not a suggestion
'Further analysis needed' — safest close
Recommendations without trade-offs
Let stakeholders decide; analysts shouldn't recommend
scenarios.hint: Does the close tell them what to do Monday morning, or just what you found?
scenarios.prompt: How do you close an analysis?
scenarios.situation: A readout ends with 'interesting patterns'. No decision is made; the work dies.
scenarios.title: The inconclusive close
scenarios.why: Close with a recommendation: the action, the evidence behind it, the trade-offs/costs, and the tripwire ('revisit if X'). 'Further analysis needed' is sometimes honest but usually abdication — say what the current evidence supports and what would change your mind. Analysis exists to drive decisions; a readout without a recommendation is entertainment.

choices: Pre-wire: share findings with key stakeholders before the big meeting, gather objections privately, adjust — the meeting ratifies, it doesn't discover
Surprise everyone in the meeting — impact
Pre-wiring is politics, not analysis
Only present to friendly audiences

scenarios.situation: A finding ('the flagship feature hurts retention') blindsides its owner in a big review. The meeting derails into methodology debate.
scenarios.title: The ambush
scenarios.why: Pre-wire controversial findings: walk key stakeholders through the analysis 1:1 before the forum — hear objections, stress-test the logic, adjust where they're right. The big meeting then decides rather than discovers. An ambush triggers defensiveness; a pre-wired finding gets a fair hearing. It's not politics — it's giving the analysis its best chance to be judged on merit.

lessons.title: SQL for Analysis — Core concepts
concepts: Time-series analysis starts by choosing the grain: DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) buckets timestamps to month starts, then GROUP BY aggregates.

DATE_TRUNC: (Syntax varies: DATE_TRUNC in Postgres, DATETRUNC in T-SQL, DATE_FORMAT in MySQL — the concept is universal.) Also mind time zones: truncate in the business's time zone, not UTC, or month boundaries shift.
COUNT(*) counts rows (events); COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts unique users. Without truncation, every distinct timestamp is its own group — noise, not trend.

Events vs users: cohort retention: group users by signup period (the cohort), then track each cohort's activity over subsequent periods — producing retention curves. 'Active users' = distinct users; 'engagement' might = events.
Cohort curves show whether newer cohorts retain better (product improving) or all cohorts decay the same (structural problem).

example.walkthrough: Time-series analysis starts by choosing the grain: DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) buckets timestamps to month starts, then GROUP BY aggregates. Without truncation, every distinct timestamp is its own group — noise, not trend.

pitfalls: Common trap: cohort analysis needs no SQL.
Common trap: cOUNT(user_id) counts unique users.
Common trap: latest row per user is impossible in SQL.
Common trap: subquery computing the grand total, joined back.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets — Core concepts
concepts: Pivot tables are the exploration tool: drag fields to rows/columns/values, slice interactively, no formula maintenance. If a pivot can't read it, it's not data, it's a picture of data.

XLOOKUP (or INDEX+MATCH): separate lookup and return arrays — looks any direction, exact match default, built-in if-not-found handling. Formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS/XLOOKUP) suit fixed, repeatable calculations that must be auditable cell-by-cell.

Data cleaning: prevent, don't fix: data validation dropdowns constrain categories, date validation constrains formats, conditional formatting flags outliers/duplicates visually, and sheet protection locks formula cells while leaving inputs editable.

lessons.title: Visualization — Core concepts
concepts: Honest axes: for segment comparison, small multiples are the most information-dense honest layout.

Chart selection: small multiples: the same chart repeated per segment, identical scales, in a grid — the eye compares shapes instantly. The chart is an argument — pick the one that makes the true pattern easiest to see.
Labeling: direct labeling (series names at line ends, values on bars) removes the legend-lookup round trip — the eye stays on the data.
Legends fail past ~4 similar series.

Color accessibility: rules: colorblind-safe palettes (blue/orange, not red/green), color never the only channel (add labels, shapes, or position), sufficient contrast for text. Then highlight: one accent color draws the eye to the insight; everything else recedes to gray.

lessons.title: Statistics — Core concepts
concepts: Skew: the mean is pulled by skew; the median (50th percentile) resists it.
Correlation vs causation: before acting on correlation: name plausible confounders, segment (does X help within engagement bands?), and run an experiment.
Confounders: rule: always segment by known confounders (device, source, region) before trusting an aggregate — the overall number can lie while every segment tells the truth.
A/B testing: proper A/B: randomize, pre-register the primary metric and runtime, size for statistical power (enough users to detect a meaningful effect), then read significance at the end.

example.code:
1000 shipments, 1% truly late (10). Test: 99% accurate.
→ ~10 true positives + ~10 false positives → P(late | flagged) ≈ 50%
example.walkthrough: With a 1% base rate, even 99% accuracy yields ~equal true and false positives (10 real lates caught, ~10 false alarms from 990 on-time). The model is fine; the expectation ignored Bayes. Lesson: rare-event prediction needs either much higher precision or a workflow that tolerates false alarms.

pitfalls: Common trap: correlation proves causation with enough data.
Common trap: A/B tests are unnecessary when correlation is strong.
Common trap: confounders don't matter with big data.
Common trap: bias only matters in small samples.

concepts: Semantic layer: a semantic layer centralizes metric definitions: one governed 'revenue' (with its exact logic, filters, and grain), consumed by all dashboards and self-service. RLS belongs in the semantic layer/platform so it's consistent across every surface.

Metric governance: dashboards are production artifacts: version their definitions (BI tools with git integration, or exported definitions in version control), document metric logic alongside, require review for certified dashboards, and keep a changelog.

Dashboard performance discipline: pre-aggregate to the dashboard's grain (materialized/aggregate tables), default to sane date ranges (not 'all time'), ensure filters hit partitioned/indexed columns, and cache.
Aggregates: a dashboard is a serving layer — it should query aggregates, not raw fact tables.

lessons.title: Data Analyst — Core concepts
concepts: Aggregate with intent: SUM, COUNT, and AVG answer 'how much' and 'how many', but always check the grain first — joining before aggregating across a one-to-many relationship silently multiplies rows.
Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, SUM ... OVER) compute across rows without collapsing them — the workhorse for rankings, running totals, and period-over-period change.
Clean before you chart: strip whitespace, fix types deliberately (zip codes are text, not numbers), remove duplicates, and document every transformation so the analysis is reproducible.
Pick the chart for the question: lines for trends over time, bars for comparisons across categories — and almost never pie, because humans judge position and length far better than angle.
Summarize skew honestly: report the median alongside the mean for skewed distributions, and never average averages that were computed on different denominators.

example.code:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS m,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT m,
       revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS mom_change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY m;
example.walkthrough: The CTE first rolls orders up to one row per month, fixing the grain before any math happens. LAG then reaches back one row in month order to compute month-over-month change — no self-join needed.

pitfalls: Common trap: COUNT(column) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) counts rows — pick the one you actually mean.
Common trap: spreadsheet auto-conversion on import (leading zeros lost, dates mangled) — import IDs as text, then convert deliberately.
Common trap: a y-axis that doesn't start at zero, exaggerating tiny differences — start at zero or annotate the break.
Common trap: presenting correlation as causation in the meeting — label it 'associated with', not 'drives'.

sections.heading: SQL for Analysis
items: Time-series analysis starts by choosing the grain — DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) buckets timestamps to month starts, then GROUP BY aggregates.

DATE_TRUNC — (Syntax varies: DATE_TRUNC in Postgres, DATETRUNC in T-SQL, DATE_FORMAT in MySQL — the concept is universal.) Also mind time zones: truncate in the business's time zone, not UTC, or month boundaries shift.
COUNT — COUNT(*) counts rows (events); COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts unique users. Without truncation, every distinct timestamp is its own group — noise, not trend.

Events vs users — cohort retention: group users by signup period (the cohort), then track each cohort's activity over subsequent periods — producing retention curves. 'Active users' = distinct users; 'engagement' might = events.
Cohort — Cohort curves show whether newer cohorts retain better (product improving) or all cohorts decay the same (structural problem).
Common trap — cohort analysis needs no SQL.
Common trap — cOUNT(user_id) counts unique users.
Common trap — latest row per user is impossible in SQL.
Common trap — subquery computing the grand total, joined back.

sections.heading: Spreadsheets
items: Pivot tables are the exploration tool — drag fields to rows/columns/values, slice interactively, no formula maintenance. If a pivot can't read it, it's not data, it's a picture of data.

XLOOKUP (or INDEX+MATCH) — separate lookup and return arrays — looks any direction, exact match default, built-in if-not-found handling. Formulas (SUMIFS/COUNTIFS/XLOOKUP) suit fixed, repeatable calculations that must be auditable cell-by-cell.

Data cleaning — prevent, don't fix: data validation dropdowns constrain categories, date validation constrains formats, conditional formatting flags outliers/duplicates visually, and sheet protection locks formula cells while leaving inputs editable.
Common trap — pivot tables can't handle large data.
Common trap — totals rows inside the data are fine.
Common trap — analyze first; cleaning is optional.
Common trap — multiple tables per sheet is tidiest.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Visualization
items: Honest axes — for segment comparison, small multiples are the most information-dense honest layout.

Chart selection — small multiples: the same chart repeated per segment, identical scales, in a grid — the eye compares shapes instantly. The chart is an argument — pick the one that makes the true pattern easiest to see.
Labeling — direct labeling (series names at line ends, values on bars) removes the legend-lookup round trip — the eye stays on the data.
Legends — Legends fail past ~4 similar series.

Color accessibility — rules: colorblind-safe palettes (blue/orange, not red/green), color never the only channel (add labels, shapes, or position), sufficient contrast for text. Then highlight: one accent color draws the eye to the insight; everything else recedes to gray.
Common trap — data-ink ratio is aesthetic trivia.
Common trap — every chart needs a border and background shading.
Common trap — axis choice doesn't affect perception.
Common trap — one chart type fits all data.

sections.heading: Statistics
items: Skew — the mean is pulled by skew; the median (50th percentile) resists it.
Correlation vs causation — before acting on correlation: name plausible confounders, segment (does X help within engagement bands?), and run an experiment.
Confounders — rule: always segment by known confounders (device, source, region) before trusting an aggregate — the overall number can lie while every segment tells the truth.
A/B testing — proper A/B: randomize, pre-register the primary metric and runtime, size for statistical power (enough users to detect a meaningful effect), then read significance at the end.
Common trap — correlation proves causation with enough data.
Common trap — A/B tests are unnecessary when correlation is strong.
Common trap — confounders don't matter with big data.
Common trap — bias only matters in small samples.

With — With a 1% base rate, even 99% accuracy yields ~equal true and false positives (10 real lates caught, ~10 false alarms from 990 on-time). The model is fine; the expectation ignored Bayes. Lesson: rare-event prediction needs either much higher precision or a…

sections.heading: BI Tools
items: Semantic layer — a semantic layer centralizes metric definitions: one governed 'revenue' (with its exact logic, filters, and grain), consumed by all dashboards and self-service. RLS belongs in the semantic layer/platform so it's consistent across every surface.

Metric governance — dashboards are production artifacts: version their definitions (BI tools with git integration, or exported definitions in version control), document metric logic alongside, require review for certified dashboards, and keep a changelog.

Dashboard performance discipline — pre-aggregate to the dashboard's grain (materialized/aggregate tables), default to sane date ranges (not 'all time'), ensure filters hit partitioned/indexed columns, and cache.
Aggregates — a dashboard is a serving layer — it should query aggregates, not raw fact tables.
Common trap — dashboards don't need version control.
Common trap — load raw billions of rows into the dashboard.
Common trap — users tolerate 2-minute dashboard loads.
Common trap — security can be handled by telling users not to look.

sections.heading: Storytelling
items: Pyramid principle — answer first ('We should do X'), then the 2-3 supporting reasons, then details as backup.
Message titles — action titles state the insight ('Enterprise churn doubled after onboarding changes'), not the content ('Churn by segment').

Communicating uncertainty — honest uncertainty: ranges instead of point estimates, key assumptions stated, sensitivity to drivers ('±3 points if renewal rate moves 5%'), and pre-mortem ('what would change this conclusion').
Narrative arc — context (what's happening), complication (the tension/change), resolution (what we should do).
Common trap — cute titles: 'Churn analysis'.
Common trap — titles should describe the chart type.
Common trap — uncertainty means the analysis failed.
Common trap — build suspense: background, methodology, then the answer on slide 20.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For SQL for Analysis: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Spreadsheets lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Visualization terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
